title: merge: Allow unlimited number of files
description:
merging is embarrassingly parallel, so long as we preserve ordering
when merging intermediate results, so we can process files in
batches if we hit RLIMIT_NOFILE and have the same output[1] we would
otherwise.

[1] One minor exception is in the SHB comments, but currently those aren't
written properly anyway. Another minor exception is that the ordering
of addresses within the NRBs can vary (be reversed), but both of these
are underlying issues, not having to do with the algorithm of batch
processing and merging.

Wireshark currently supports merging lots of files at once through
drag and drop, but not through the File->Merge dialog; we might
want to change the latter.

Fix #17598

notes.body: "Note that Wireshark currently doesn't support merging lots of files at once" any plans? :D

> "Note that Wireshark currently doesn't support merging lots of files at once" any plans?

Presumably that would involve one or more of 1) allowing multiple files to be selected in the File > Merge dialog and 2) handling a user dragging and dropping a set of multiple files into the currently-open file.  (macOS, at least, lets you select multiple files and drop them into a Wireshark window.  I didn't check whether it merges all those files into the current capture or not.)

That would also require some UI mechanism that allows selecting "lots of files" conveniently; those may be a function of the OS/desktop environment.

That would, of course, happen to be done atop *this* change, which is purely a change to the libwiretap code that implements file merging, and which both the mergecap command and Wireshark use.
On UN\*Xes, should the merge code try raising the file descriptor limit itself, and only do it in multiple batches if the *hard* limit is too low?
On recent Linux, `OPEN_MAX` is not defined, even if `limits.h` is included, and `sysconf(_SC_OPEN_MAX)` returns the soft limit of open files.
https://gitlab.winehq.org/wine/wine/-/blob/master/dlls/ntdll/unix/loader.c?ref_type=heads

> From what I've read, on at least some versions of MacOS (Leopard and later, maybe fixed in recent version, this doesn't succeed if `rl.rlim_max > OPEN_MAX`

Intentional, not a bug, so not something to be fixed.  I think it "succeeds" in the sense that `setrlimit()` returns 0 in that case, and `getrlimit()` might even return the hard limit after that, but every time the system checks the limit, it's checked against the minimum of the nominal limit and the separately-defined absolute limit.

The absolute limit is a `sysctl()` value, kern.maxfilesperproc.  Its initial value is `OPEN_MAX`.  It *could* be increased with the `sysctl` command (or by `sysctl()` calls), but both may require root privileges to increase.

> macOS, at least, lets you select multiple files and drop them into a Wireshark window. I didn't check whether it merges all those files into the current capture or not.

Huh, that does work, including on Linux. I didn't know that would work.

It does not merge all the those files into the current capture; it replaces the currently open capture with the result of merging all the selected files. The File -> Merge menu doesn't (at least on Linux) allow selecting more than one file.

So I guess in the case of dragging and dropping a large number of files, this should help too. I suppose I should edit the comment.

> The File -> Merge menu doesn't (at least on Linux) allow selecting more than one file.

That's a Qt file selection dialog, except on Windows (where we pop up a native Windows dialog).  [The Qt 6.x version](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qfiledialog.html), and [the Qt 5.x version](https://doc.qt.io/qt-5/qfiledialog.html), at least, have [a `setFileMode` method](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qfiledialog.html#fileMode-prop) that allows it to be set to [`QFileDialog::ExistingFiles`](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qfiledialog.html#FileMode-enum), plural, which allows the dialog to return "The names of zero or more existing files.".  That enum "is used to indicate what the user may select in the file dialog", so setting it to `QFileDialog::ExistingFiles` may allow multiple files to be selected.  The code that pops up that dialog may have to be changed to *handle* a list of multiple file names.

That should make it happen on all platforms other than Windows.  For Windows, you'd have to modify the code that pops up the native dialog.

> The absolute limit is a `sysctl()` value, kern.maxfilesperproc. Its initial value is `OPEN_MAX`. It *could* be increased with the `sysctl` command (or by `sysctl()` calls), but both may require root privileges to increase.

Also true in FreeBSD, but there it appears that the values passed to `setrlimit()` will silently be clipped at kern.maxfilesperproc, rather than the clipping being done when the limit is checked.  The same appears to apply in DragonFly BSD.

Similar in NetBSD, but it calls the `sysctl()` value kern.maxfiles (which appears to be the name for the system-wide limit, rather than the per-process, in DragonFly BSD).  OpenBSD may be similar.

> I think it "succeeds" in the sense that setrlimit() returns 0 in that case,

What the developers of Wine said is that on certain versions (Leopard until Big Sur, perhaps) `setrlimit()` returns -1 in such cases where you pass in a value greater than the separately defined absolute limit, but that at some point it was corrected to the behavior you describe, that also all the BSD flavors do. At least that's how I read this: https://gitlab.winehq.org/wine/wine/-/commit/de7604b6c68e2e69c1f56d20e34d13639c7a4ea1

Probably the safest thing to do is to remember if we have already checked and tried to raise the limit once and not try again, to avoid any possible infinite loop if there's any OS version where `setrlimit()` returns 0, but `getrlimit()` later still claims that the soft limit is less than the hard limit.

commits_data.title: merge: Try to raise the soft limit of open files on UN*X
commits_data.message:
merge: Try to raise the soft limit of open files on UN*X

If get an EMFILE on UN*X, try to raise the soft limit for the
number of open file descriptors if it's less than the hard limit.
Raise it to the minimum of what we need and the hard limit.

On macOS before Big Sur, you can't always raise the soft limit to
the current hard limit as returned by getrlimit, because that can
be set to, e.g., RLIM_INFINITY even when there's an effective lower
limit set by kern.maxfilesperproc on sysctl (Mojave to Monterey)
or the possibly lower fixed limit OPEN_MAX (10240) from Leopard
until some version before Mojave.

Use a workaround for this based on some from Wine.
